“The Anthropic IPO is attracting gobs of attention,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager ⁠at Argent Capital in St. Louis, Missouri.
Even so, Ellerbroek’s enthusiasm for ‌the AI trade has waned.

“My beliefs about the growth in data centre capex spending have come down a little bit over the last month or two,” he added. “Nvidia’s crisis situation is a big deal. The midterm elections have had an impact. Data centres are ‌going to be more expensive to build and they’re going to be built more ​slowly.”
Advanced Micro Devices shares tumbled after investigative outlet Hunterbrook said its affiliated fund, Hunterbrook Capital, had taken a short position in the company.
Most chipmakers were ⁠lower, including Micron and Broadcom, among others.
Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment.

articles.title: Draft of COP31 cover text drops references to fossil fuel phase-out, net zero dates
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A major concern raised by developing countries, of phasing out unilateral trade measures such as the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) by 2027, that was present in the earlier draft has also been eliminated

The latest iteration of the COP 31 draft cover text has eliminated references to fossil fuel phase-out and net-zero dates but has also deleted references to a firm $120 billion adaptation-finance target that developing countries have been asking for as “legally binding financial obligations” on developed countries. This suggests that the most ambitious demands of both the developed and developing country blocs have been eliminated.

A cover text is an overarching political decision that frames the outcome of a climate conference rather than settling any single agenda item. It is usually finalised last, and like every outcome it needs the consensus of all Parties. The Presidency has said earlier drafts were not meant to reflect consensus.

The COP31 Presidency’s revised draft cover decision, dated November 19, has 80 paragraphs, down from 144 in the November 16 version. The summit officially ends on November 20, though negotiations frequently overshoot into the weekend.

A major concern raised by developing countries, of phasing out unilateral trade measures such as the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) by 2027, that was present in the earlier draft has also been eliminated.

However, a widely expected outcome of raising electricity’s share in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, scaling up the use of carbon capture utilisation technologies and making early warning systems universal by 2027, continue to find mention in the text. A broad commitment to triple adaptation finance also remains.

“ The draft cover text weaves the 35% electricity in final energy consumption by 2035, alongside tripling renewable energy capacity and doubling the rate of energy efficiency improvement by 2030, ” Ajay Mathur, India’s lead negotiator at Paris COP and former DG, International Solar Alliance, said in a statement. The electricity use in India went up by 13% in 2025 due to the Hormuz crisis alone. It will be an ambitious goal for India to achieve 35% electrification by 2035, but due to the increasing amount of renewable energy in the Indian energy mix, we will be near the 32-34% mark by 2035. ”

“We’re down to the wire at COP31, and the latest texts are alarmingly far from ambitious or equitable,” said Rachel Cleetus, Climate Program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) in a statement. “Rich nations, most notably the EU nations, are still holding a harsh line against committing to tripling adaptation finance to at least $120 billion annually by 2035. Instead of reaching agreement on urgently needed climate finance, some countries seem willing to push negotiations toward failure.”

A major concern raised by developing countries, of phasing out unilateral trade measures such as the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) by 2027, that was present in the earlier draft has also been eliminated

The latest iteration of the COP 31 draft cover text has eliminated references to fossil fuel phase-out and net-zero dates but has also deleted references to a firm $120 billion adaptation-finance target that developing countries have been asking for as “legally binding financial obligations” on developed countries. This suggests that the most ambitious demands of both the developed and developing country blocs have been eliminated.

A cover text is an overarching political decision that frames the outcome of a climate conference rather than settling any single agenda item. It is usually finalised last, and like every outcome it needs the consensus of all Parties. The Presidency has said earlier drafts were not meant to reflect consensus.

The COP31 Presidency’s revised draft cover decision, dated November 19, has 80 paragraphs, down from 144 in the November 16 version. The summit officially ends on November 20, though negotiations frequently overshoot into the weekend.

A major concern raised by developing countries, of phasing out unilateral trade measures such as the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) by 2027, that was present in the earlier draft has also been eliminated.

However, a widely expected outcome of raising electricity’s share in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, scaling up the use of carbon capture utilisation technologies and making early warning systems universal by 2027, continue to find mention in the text. A broad commitment to triple adaptation finance also remains.

“ The draft cover text weaves the 35% electricity in final energy consumption by 2035, alongside tripling renewable energy capacity and doubling the rate of energy efficiency improvement by 2030, ” Ajay Mathur, India’s lead negotiator at Paris COP and former DG, International Solar Alliance, said in a statement. The electricity use in India went up by 13% in 2025 due to the Hormuz crisis alone. It will be an ambitious goal for India to achieve 35% electrification by 2035, but due to the increasing amount of renewable energy in the Indian energy mix, we will be near the 32-34% mark by 2035. ”

“We’re down to the wire at COP31, and the latest texts are alarmingly far from ambitious or equitable,” said Rachel Cleetus, Climate Program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) in a statement. “Rich nations, most notably the EU nations, are still holding a harsh line against committing to tripling adaptation finance to at least $120 billion annually by 2035. Instead of reaching agreement on urgently needed climate finance, some countries seem willing to push negotiations toward failure.”

articles.title: Talks without peace: On Russia, Ukraine, U.S. talks
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Europe must be part of any settlement on the Ukraine war

The trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. earlier this month failed to produce a major breakthrough or bridge the wide gap between Kyiv and Moscow. Yet, they were a good beginning towards finding a political settlement to Europe’s longest war since the Second World War . In the two-day talks, hosted by the U.S., the warring sides agreed on some humanitarian measures, including prisoner exchange. U.S. representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow after the talks to discuss the proposal. In the next stage, U.S., Ukrainian and European officials will meet in Berlin to discuss a coordinated European and Ukrainian position towards the peace process. As of now, Russian and Ukrainian positions remain far apart. Russia demands Ukraine withdraw from the territories of Donbas it still controls to stop attacks. Russia also wants to introduce limits to Ukrainian military capabilities and Kyiv to declare neutrality (give up its NATO ambitions). Ukraine, on the other hand, has rejected making any territorial concessions for a settlement and asked for security guarantees from the West so that Russia would not attack the country again.

That Ukraine survived Russia’s invasion and continued to resist Russian forces for almost five years is no small feat. But it has also paid a huge price for its resistance. The country has lost more than 20% of its territory. Millions have fled, while men of fighting age are being drafted into the military . Ukraine’s economy is kept afloat by European support, while its military continues to rely on NATO for weapons and other supplies. Until recently, the West stood united in its support for Ukraine against Russia, but that unity has since begun to fray. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel, is seeking to reset Washington’s ties with Moscow . European leaders, who initially sought to isolate Russia, have also started reestablishing contacts with the Kremlin. In October, Finnish and Norwegian leaders held direct talks with Mr. Putin. To be sure, Ukraine’s long-range strikes can hurt Russia, as the recent attack on the Kerch Bridge demonstrated. But such strikes are unlikely to change the Kremlin’s thinking about the war. As the conflict drags on, Ukraine’s position is weakening, and its allies are growing increasingly divided. After almost five years, Russia has failed to take a decisive victory. Ukraine does not have a credible path towards victory either. A diplomatic settlement, therefore, is the only way forward. The Abu Dhabi talks recognised this reality. But for the process to be meaningful, Europe must also be brought to the negotiating table.

articles.title: Vinita Zutshi brings Kashmir’s forgotten folktales to young readers
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Author and storyteller Vinita Zutshi revisits Kashmir’s oral traditions in a collection of 18 folktales, bringing its characters, customs and storytelling heritage to a new generation of readers

The absence of a familiar story can sometimes reveal how much of a culture has slipped out of everyday conversation. For author and storyteller Vinita Zutshi, that realisation came while she was conducting storytelling sessions in Kashmir. “Teachers spoke to me about children who could no longer speak Kashmiri. The families acknowledged that many of the stories passed down by their elders had never been recorded,” says Vinita. The discovery eventually became the starting point for a literary exercise that would take her into the world of Kashmiri folklore.

Her book, Folktales from Kashmir , brings together 18 traditional narratives that have travelled through generations, largely through oral storytelling. Published under Red Panda, the children’s literature imprint of Westland Books, it is a 178-page illustrated collection. Illustrated by Charbak Dipta, the book introduces young readers to an assortment of characters, including foolish kings, clever tricksters, ambitious old women, daring daughters, jackals and unlucky thieves. The stories combine humour, everyday situations and elements of magic, with observations on human behaviour woven into their narratives.

She subsequently began looking for people who could share these narratives. Conversations with families revealed that parents and grandparents had carried the stories in their memories, but few had thought of preserving them in the written form. One interaction with a student, who spoke about her mother collecting stories in a village near Pulwama, particularly surprised her. “She was a repository of fascinating stories. Eventually, I came across another elderly woman who shared her own collection of tales, and that is how my journey of discovering and documenting Kashmiri folktales began,” she recalls.
Author and storyteller Vinita Zutshi who revisits Kashmir’s oral traditions in a collection of 18 folktales. She will be a part of Vizag Junior Literary Festival. | Photo Credit: SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT

The project has a personal dimension for Vinita, who describes her engagement with Kashmiri folklore as a process of discovering her own cultural inheritance and her Kashmiri roots. “I grew up across different parts of the country, but Kashmiri was not spoken at home by my parents. English and Hindi became our languages of communication,” she says. Her interest in collecting these stories grew from an awareness that a considerable body of traditional knowledge remained undocumented.

The collection also reflects her interest in the way traditional stories engage with human nature. Vinita points out that folktales rarely depend on flawless heroes. Their characters are recognisably human, with practical concerns, ambitions, weaknesses and occasional lapses in judgement. “Not all heroes have to be strong. The characters in Kashmiri folktales are very practical and rooted in everyday realities. They have their own shortcomings, and that is what makes them interesting,” adds Vinita. Some narratives have unexpected turns, while others use humour to examine greed, vanity and the consequences of one’s choices.

For Vinita, this range of emotions is particularly relevant to contemporary childhood. “Resilience is missing in children today. Parents are often unwilling to talk about difficult emotions and tend to step in at every instance of discomfort,” she says. Stories, she feels, can gently introduce children to situations involving disappointment, uncertainty and difficult choices. Classic fairy tales such as Hansel and Gretel and Cinderella have characters and settings that may feel culturally distant to Indian children. Folktales rooted in Indian traditions, she argues, give them another cultural context through which to explore similar experiences.

An author of 22 books, Vinita is also a performance storyteller, editor, speaker and transformational parenting coach. Her storytelling performances, which she has presented to audiences in India and abroad, rely on voice, expression and characterisation rather than puppets or props. She believes that an audience should be able to see an entire story unfold through the spoken word.

Vinita will bring this approach to Visakhapatnam at the seventh edition of the Vizag Junior Literary Festival on November 21 and 22 at Hawa Mahal, Beach Road. Her storytelling sessions will offer young participants an opportunity to experience the oral tradition and engage with stories through performance.

For Vinita, the larger purpose of sharing these narratives is to keep stories in circulation. “A folktale survives when someone chooses to tell it again and when another generation finds a reason to listen,” she adds.

🏛️ Political, National & Polity 📅 20 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 6 Min Read

📰 Vinita Zutshi brings Kashmir’s forgotten folktales to young readers

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes

Author and storyteller Vinita Zutshi revisits Kashmir’s oral traditions in a collection of 18 folktales, bringing its characters, customs and storytelling heritage to a new generation of readers

The absence of a familiar story can sometimes reveal how much of a culture has slipped out of everyday conversation. For author and storyteller Vinita Zutshi, that realisation came while she was conducting storytelling sessions in Kashmir. “Teachers spoke to me about children who could no longer speak Kashmiri. The families acknowledged that many of the stories passed down by their elders had never been recorded,” says Vinita. The discovery eventually became the starting point for a literary exercise that would take her into the world of Kashmiri folklore.

Her book, Folktales from Kashmir , brings together 18 traditional narratives that have travelled through generations, largely through oral storytelling. Published under Red Panda, the children’s literature imprint of Westland Books, it is a 178-page illustrated collection. Illustrated by Charbak Dipta, the book introduces young readers to an assortment of characters, including foolish kings, clever tricksters, ambitious old women, daring daughters, jackals and unlucky thieves. The stories combine humour, everyday situations and elements of magic, with observations on human behaviour woven into their narratives.

She subsequently began looking for people who could share these narratives. Conversations with families revealed that parents and grandparents had carried the stories in their memories, but few had thought of preserving them in the written form. One interaction with a student, who spoke about her mother collecting stories in a village near Pulwama, particularly surprised her. “She was a repository of fascinating stories. Eventually, I came across another elderly woman who shared her own collection of tales, and that is how my journey of discovering and documenting Kashmiri folktales began,” she recalls.

Author and storyteller Vinita Zutshi who revisits Kashmir’s oral traditions in a collection of 18 folktales. She will be a part of Vizag Junior Literary Festival. | Photo Credit: SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT

The project has a personal dimension for Vinita, who describes her engagement with Kashmiri folklore as a process of discovering her own cultural inheritance and her Kashmiri roots. “I grew up across different parts of the country, but Kashmiri was not spoken at home by my parents. English and Hindi became our languages of communication,” she says. Her interest in collecting these stories grew from an awareness that a considerable body of traditional knowledge remained undocumented.

The collection also reflects her interest in the way traditional stories engage with human nature. Vinita points out that folktales rarely depend on flawless heroes. Their characters are recognisably human, with practical concerns, ambitions, weaknesses and occasional lapses in judgement. “Not all heroes have to be strong. The characters in Kashmiri folktales are very practical and rooted in everyday realities. They have their own shortcomings, and that is what makes them interesting,” adds Vinita. Some narratives have unexpected turns, while others use humour to examine greed, vanity and the consequences of one’s choices.

For Vinita, this range of emotions is particularly relevant to contemporary childhood. “Resilience is missing in children today. Parents are often unwilling to talk about difficult emotions and tend to step in at every instance of discomfort,” she says. Stories, she feels, can gently introduce children to situations involving disappointment, uncertainty and difficult choices. Classic fairy tales such as Hansel and Gretel and Cinderella have characters and settings that may feel culturally distant to Indian children. Folktales rooted in Indian traditions, she argues, give them another cultural context through which to explore similar experiences.

An author of 22 books, Vinita is also a performance storyteller, editor, speaker and transformational parenting coach. Her storytelling performances, which she has presented to audiences in India and abroad, rely on voice, expression and characterisation rather than puppets or props. She believes that an audience should be able to see an entire story unfold through the spoken word.

Vinita will bring this approach to Visakhapatnam at the seventh edition of the Vizag Junior Literary Festival on November 21 and 22 at Hawa Mahal, Beach Road. Her storytelling sessions will offer young participants an opportunity to experience the oral tradition and engage with stories through performance.

For Vinita, the larger purpose of sharing these narratives is to keep stories in circulation. “A folktale survives when someone chooses to tell it again and when another generation finds a reason to listen,” she adds.

The discovery eventually became the starting point for a literary exercise that would take her into the world of Kashmiri folklore.

articles.title: FSSAI licences suspended of two Karachi Bakery units in Hyderabad, four meat outlets over food safety violations
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The action was part of a special enforcement drive conducted on Thursday (November 19, 2026) by 11 teams comprising Food Safety Officers and police personnel

The Telangana Standards Authority for Food and Essential Drugs (TG SAFE) has suspended the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) licences of six establishments, including two units linked to Karachi Bakery in Hyderabad, following inspections that exposed serious food safety violations.

The establishments include Karachi INC in Srinagar Colony, Karachi Bakery Pearl Private Limited at Gaganpahad, Watan Traders in Musheerabad, Punjab Fish Company in Secunderabad, Hi Protein on SD Road and SM SEA Corporation in Uppal. All six have been directed to immediately stop business operations in the interest of public health.

The action was part of a special enforcement drive conducted on Thursday (November 19, 2026) by 11 teams comprising Food Safety Officers and police personnel. The teams inspected 15 meat retail and processing units and four Karachi Bakery manufacturing units across Hyderabad and its outskirts.

The violations detected at units associated with Karachi Bakery include pest infestation, cobwebs, rat droppings, rusty baking trays, defective machinery, unclean refrigerators in the cake section, cleaning chemicals stored alongside food articles and clogged kitchen drains. Officials seized 1,012 kg of packed food products worth ₹4.34 lakh from the Gaganpahad unit.

The violations at other four establishments, which were meat shops, include slaughtering waste found discarded or stored in unhygienic conditions, clogged drains in its processing areas, raw fish and prawns exposed to flies, expired frozen prawns were found in storage, dead flies inside a freezer.

Separately, TG SAFE seized approximately 1,672 kg of food articles worth ₹6.59 lakh during the inspections and ordered five meat retail and processing establishments to shut down for operating without FSSAI licences and maintaining unhygienic conditions. They include Anand Mutton and Chicken Point at Shankarmat in Nallakunta, Salman KGN Poultry and New Decent Meat Chicken and Fish Shop at Erragadda, Protein Foods on SP Road in Secunderabad and AP Fisheries Fish Stall at Goutham Nagar Road in Malkajgiri.

Improvement notices will be issued to Watan Fresh Mart in Musheerabad and Metro Cash and Carry India Limited at Uppal, directing them to rectify the deficiencies. The establishments will be reinspected to verify compliance.

Additionally, show-cause notices will also be issued to 10 establishments, including Metro Cash and Carry outlets at Gaganpahad, Moosapet and Suchitra X Road, Sai Baba Inc (Karachi Bakery) at M.J. Market in Goshamahal and Licious at Kistapur village in Medchal mandal, along with the five establishments ordered to shut down. Further action, including penalties, will be initiated based on the violations, TG SAFE said.

articles.title: Indonesian fire emissions third highest on record this year, says EU’s Copernicus
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: This year’s fires in Indonesia produced nearly 200 million metric tonnes of carbon emissions ​by November 15, the European Union’s climate monitoring service ‌said

This year’s fires in Indonesia produced nearly 200 million metric tonnes of carbon emissions ​by November 15, the European Union’s climate monitoring service ‌said on Thursday (November 19, 2026), the third-highest annual volume on ​record.
* The archipelago has suffered its ⁠worst wildfire season in years, driven by excessively dry super-El Niño weather conditions and warmer temperatures, as well as extensive ‌land clearing

* Total fire emissions fell short of the record of nearly 400 million tonnes ‌in 2015 and were also slightly lower than ‌in ⁠2006, another strong El Niño year, ⁠according to the EU’s Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), which tracks fire emission records dating back to 2003

* This year’s fire emissions ​were the equivalent of ‌more than a fifth of Indonesia’s total carbon footprint in 2025, with the country’s energy consumption and industry responsible for an estimated 960 million tonnes ‌of CO2 last year, according to the Statistical ​Review of World Energy
* Emissions generated by Indonesia’s fires were also around the same ⁠as the entire energy and industrial carbon footprint of Pakistan last year

* CAMS data showed that nearly ‌8.9 million hectares (22 million acres) of land could have been damaged by fire in Indonesia this year, 4.7% of its total area, significantly higher than the 2012 to 2025 average of 1.9%.

* The figure is significantly higher than the 2.9-million-hectare estimate ‌for January to October provided last week by geomonitoring platform ​Nusantara Atlas, which uses a more conservative methodology
* Though El Niño-driven drought was a decisive ⁠factor in this year’s fires, experts have also emphasised ⁠the role played by climate change in driving up temperatures
* Poor land management and the ‌excessive draining of peatland to make way for palm oil or pulpwood concessions have also made ​Indonesia more vulnerable to fire.

This year’s fires in Indonesia produced nearly 200 million metric tonnes of carbon emissions ​by November 15, the European Union’s climate monitoring service ‌said

This year’s fires in Indonesia produced nearly 200 million metric tonnes of carbon emissions ​by November 15, the European Union’s climate monitoring service ‌said on Thursday (November 19, 2026), the third-highest annual volume on ​record.

* The archipelago has suffered its ⁠worst wildfire season in years, driven by excessively dry super-El Niño weather conditions and warmer temperatures, as well as extensive ‌land clearing

* Total fire emissions fell short of the record of nearly 400 million tonnes ‌in 2015 and were also slightly lower than ‌in ⁠2006, another strong El Niño year, ⁠according to the EU’s Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), which tracks fire emission records dating back to 2003

* This year’s fire emissions ​were the equivalent of ‌more than a fifth of Indonesia’s total carbon footprint in 2025, with the country’s energy consumption and industry responsible for an estimated 960 million tonnes ‌of CO2 last year, according to the Statistical ​Review of World Energy

* Emissions generated by Indonesia’s fires were also around the same ⁠as the entire energy and industrial carbon footprint of Pakistan last year

* CAMS data showed that nearly ‌8.9 million hectares (22 million acres) of land could have been damaged by fire in Indonesia this year, 4.7% of its total area, significantly higher than the 2012 to 2025 average of 1.9%.

* The figure is significantly higher than the 2.9-million-hectare estimate ‌for January to October provided last week by geomonitoring platform ​Nusantara Atlas, which uses a more conservative methodology

* Though El Niño-driven drought was a decisive ⁠factor in this year’s fires, experts have also emphasised ⁠the role played by climate change in driving up temperatures

* Poor land management and the ‌excessive draining of peatland to make way for palm oil or pulpwood concessions have also made ​Indonesia more vulnerable to fire.

articles.title: Cheetah brought from Botswana gives birth to four cubs at Kuno
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: With these four new arrivals, India’s cheetah population has risen to 62, including 43 Indian-born individuals

A two-and-a-half-year-old cheetah, KOMG 3, brought from Botswana, gave birth to four healthy cubs in the wild at Madhya Pradesh’s Kuno National Park on Friday (November 20, 2026), Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav said.
Calling the development a matter of pride for Madhya Pradesh and the entire country, Chief Minister Mohan Yadav said it was a historic achievement for Project Cheetah.
In a post on X, Bhupender Yadav said KOMG 3 is the first cheetah from Botswana to give birth in India.
“This is a landmark moment for Project Cheetah and a proud milestone in India’s journey towards restoring a viable cheetah population,” he added.
This is the second recorded birth in the wild since the reintroduction programme began in 2022.
With these four new arrivals, India’s cheetah population has risen to 62, including 43 Indian-born individuals.
“Every such birth strengthens our hope, deepens our commitment, and reminds us that conservation is a journey of patience, perseverance and collective effort,” Mr. Yadav said.
He also acknowledged the dedication, commitment and hard work of project managers, veterinarians, frontline forest staff and everyone working tirelessly for the success of Project Cheetah.

In a statement, CM Mohan Yadav said, “This is a matter of pride for Madhya Pradesh and the entire country. The birth of cubs in India for the first time by a female cheetah from Botswana is a historic achievement of Project Cheetah.

“This is an important and encouraging step towards restoring a viable cheetah population in India. KOMG 3, a female cheetah, gave birth to four healthy cubs in natural conditions after spending more than four months in the wild.”

articles.title: Bhavani Mandala Deeksha begins at Kanaka Durga temple in Vijayawada
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Devotees can receive the sacred mala at Indrakeeladri from November 20 to 24, the temple’s Vedic Committee says

The Bhavani Mandala Deeksha Mahotsavam-2026 commenced on a devotional note at the Sri Durga Malleswara Swamy Varla Devasthanam atop Indrakeeladri, the abode of Goddess Kanaka Durga, in Vijayawada on Friday (November 20, 2026), with a good number of devotees from different parts of the State taking up the spiritual vow on the first day.

The rituals began on the auspicious occasion of ‘Karthika Shuddha Ekadasi’ with the installation of the idol of Goddess Bhavani on the sixth floor of the temple’s Maha Mandapam. The processional deity was brought from the main temple in a ceremonial procession accompanied by Vedic chants and traditional music.
The deity was decorated with floral and beaded garlands and installed on a specially arranged pedestal amid traditional lamps and offerings.

Devotees carry the processional deity of Goddess Bhavani in a palanquin to the Maha Mandapam on Indrakeeladri in Vijayawada on Friday, the first day of the Bhavani Mandala Deeksha. | Photo Credit: K.V.S. Giri
Temple priests performed special rituals under the supervision of temple Sthanacharya V. Siva Prasad Sharma and chief priest Kota Prasad.

Following the rituals, Deputy Chief Priest Nagaraju Sastry initiated devotees into the ‘deeksha’ by conferring the sacred ‘mala’ . Men, women and children, many dressed in traditional crimson attire, participated in the rituals. Hundreds of devotees gathered at the hill shrine for ‘mala dharana’ and darshan. The temple premises reverberated with chants of the name of Goddess Bhavani.
The ceremonial proceedings, including the procession of priests and temple officials in front of the temple’s multi-tiered gopuram, added to the festive atmosphere at Indrakeeladri.
Devotees carry the processional deity of Goddess Bhavani in a palanquin to the Maha Mandapam on Indrakeeladri in Vijayawada on Friday. | Photo Credit: K.V.S. Giri

Devotees undertaking the Bhavani Deeksha observe prescribed austerities, including a simple vegetarian diet and traditional dress, for the duration of their vow. The observance may be undertaken for a ‘Mandala’ or ‘Ardha Mandala’ period and concludes with the prescribed deeksha-ending rituals.
According to the temple’s Vedic Committee, devotees wishing to undertake the Bhavani Mandala Deeksha can receive the sacred mala at Indrakeeladri from November 20 to 24.

articles.title: NHAI’s AI tool to monitor road damage, follow-up complaints with contractors
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) is deploying an artificial intelligence-powered analytical tool to assess road conditions, identify damage to roads and pavements, communicate the information to contractors, follow up on the complaints and ensure that the issues are rectified.

As a part of a series of technical sessions at the 85th Indian Roads Congress in Hyderabad, NHAI officials said Dashcam Analytics systems had been mounted in patrol vehicles to monitor highways for infrastructure-related issues. The system captures geotagged, high-resolution photographs of road conditions, pavements and road signage and uploads them to a dashboard. Each photograph is uniquely numbered. The system then communicates the information to the relevant contractor, who proceeds to rectify the issue. NHAI officials described it as an end-to-end “detection to rectification” system.

Key road conditions identified by the system include potholes and road rutting, which refers to the formation of depressed surfaces on the road. Other issues identified include edge dropping and uneven road shoulders, streetlights that are not working, signage, and gaps in road medians.

The IRC also deliberated on whether India could take a lead in road safety globally. Samrat Valani, vice-president of Development, Operations and Customer Experience, North America, Transurban, made a case for a clear mandate to halve road deaths by 2030, in line with the Stockholm Declaration on road safety adopted in 2020. He emphasised the need for a strong framework based on the “four Es”: education, engineering, enforcement and emergency care, along with political will and evidence that the initiatives were working.

Sharing examples of road safety interventions from across the world, he said that data show that in India, 54,000 people who were did not wear helmets lost their lives in last year. Citing the case of Vietnam, which he described as a “motorcycle country”, he said a government led awareness programme at around 100 schools had increased helmet use from 36% to 69% in one year.

“As the programme continued, they saw in the next year that the usage dropped to 50% and stabilised at around 57%. The point here is not the number of injuries, but the helmet use and the ability to count. What this gives us is that when you count, you get to know the effectiveness of the programme,” he said.

Touching upon the importance of quick incident and accident detection, leveraging technology to respond to incidents and clearing them as quickly as possible, he said that in the US, for every minute an incident remains on the roadway, the likelihood of a secondary accident increases by 2.8%.

Informing road users, creating awareness and measuring outcomes, adopting a fair approach by issuing warnings, particularly in cases of speeding, followed by firm enforcement, and using data to prevent crashes are important metrics, he said.

articles.title: Supreme Court dismisses Karnataka appeal against bike-taxis
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: A Bench headed by Justice Satish Chandra Sharma said regulation was better than a blanket ban

The Supreme Court on Friday (November 20, 2026) dismissed an appeal by the Karnataka State government challenging a State High Court decision to allow bike-taxis as public transport, removing the brakes on taxi aggregators like Ola, Uber, and Rapido from offering two-wheeler taxi services in the State.
From August 2026: Bike taxi association seeks halt to crackdown, urges clear policy framework

A Bench headed by Justice Satish Chandra Sharma said regulation was better than a blanket ban. The judge said even the staff in his office opt to travel by bike-taxi rather than autorickshaws and cabs due to the considerable fare difference.
The judge noted that bike-taxis with GPS were safer for women, and two-wheeler taxis are already operating across 25 States.

The Karnataka government had found bike-taxis dangerous, saying they were not meant for public transport, considering the low safety standards of motorcycles and higher accident fatality rates. The State, represented by advocate Sanchit Garga, argued that the restriction on using two-wheelers as taxis was reasonable, proportionate, and in the public interest.

“The State has not imposed a blanket prohibition on the use of motorcycles for commercial purposes; rather, it has only restricted their use for carrying passengers. Motorcycle riders continue to have viable alternative avenues of livelihood, including under the Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act, 2025, which provides statutory protection and welfare measures for such workers,” Karnataka submitted.

A Division Bench of the High Court, in January 2026, set aside a Single Bench order from April last year, which stopped bike-taxi services pending the framing of a policy by the State. articles.title: Karnataka govt. to invest on Hassan airport, even as operations face uncertainty in other district airports
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The demand for an airport in Hassan, about 190 km from Bengaluru, goes back more than six decades. Work has progressed at a snail’s pace, though land acquisition began as early as 1966. Work on the ground began in 2021, but has shown hardly any progress

The Karnataka Cabinet has decided to expand the Hassan airport project at a time when flight operations at other airports, including Shivamogga, face an uncertain future. An airport for Hassan has been in the pipeline for several decades.

Incidentally, Star Air, the private operator, ended its flights from Shivamogga Airport under the UDAN scheme on Friday (November 20, 2026), as the three-year subsidy period came to an end. The airline will continue to take bookings for the weekend on the Hyderabad route only, at commercial fares, without subsidy.

On Thursday, the Cabinet approved a revised cost of ₹542.96 crore for the project, up from the ₹193.65 crore sanctioned in 2021. It cleared an additional ₹349.31 crore, of which ₹122 crore is for acquiring more land and ₹227.31 crore for additional works and the facilities needed to operate the airport.

Excise Minister and Hassan in-charge Minister K.M. Shivalinge Gowda has held meetings to speed up land acquisition, which has held up the work. He has said he aims to start flights from Hassan within two years and to inaugurate the airport before his term ends.

The demand for an airport in Hassan, about 190 km from Bengaluru, goes back more than six decades. Work has progressed at a snail’s pace, though land acquisition began as early as 1966. Work on the ground began in 2021 but has shown hardly any progress in the last two years.

The first proposal for the airport was prepared by the Central Public Works Department in 1960. In November 1966, 31 acres 31 guntas of private land and 58 acres of government land were acquired for the project. In the second phase, another 12 acres of private land and 42 acres of government land were acquired in 1971.

The project received attention during the JD(S)-BJP coalition government headed by H.D. Kumaraswamy. Former Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda laid the foundation stone in 2007, after the government signed an agreement with Jupiter Aviation Services Pvt. Ltd. for construction on the build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) model.

However, the work did not move forward. The project proponent had planned additional activities, including a golf course and a hotel, and refused to start work until the entire 960 acres required for the project was handed over. The agreement with the private firm was cancelled in 2018, when the JD(S) came to power again, this time with the Congress.

When B.S. Yediyurappa became Chief Minister, he announced ₹175 crore for the airport in his 2021 budget. The Karnataka State Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation (KSIIDC) was the project implementing agency. The project has now been revised.

Meanwhile, KSIIDC Chairman S.G. Nanjayyanamath questioned the viability of airports in tier-II and tier-III cities such as Hassan and Raichur. Hassan is only two-and-a-half to three hours from Bengaluru by road, he noted, and asked whether people would choose to fly such a short distance. He raised similar doubts about Raichur. “I am not opposed to constructing airports in these cities. But I wish there were a discussion on the viability of investing so much money in such projects,” he said during a recent visit to Shivamogga.

articles.title: Replace Russian junk with American weapons system: U.S. lawmaker to India
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Michael Baumgartner made the remarks on Capitol Hill in the presence of Namgya Khampa, the Deputy Chief of Mission at the Indian Embassy in Washington

India should replace its "legacy ineffective Russian junk” with American weapons systems and also opt for Boeing aircraft over those manufactured by European Airbus Industries, a U.S. Congressman has suggested.

Michael Baumgartner, a Republican from Washington state, made the remarks at Deepavali celebrations on Capitol Hill on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) in the presence of Namgya Khampa, the Deputy Chief of Mission at the Indian Embassy in Washington.

The Deepavali celebrations were hosted by BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha, Asian American Hotel Owners Association, Hindu American Foundations, Srimad Rajchandra Mission Dharampur, Sikhs of America, Art of Living, Foundations of Jain Associations in North America and the U.S. Indian Community Foundation.

As a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Mr. Baumgartner said he regularly engages with diplomats from the Indian Embassy as the two countries seek to strengthen relations across economic and security issues.

“I was pleased to again express my thoughts that the more U.S. exports to India — from weapons systems to replace their legacy ineffective Russian junk to Boeing airplanes that are superior to Airbus to the world’s best lentils from the Palouse — the better it is for our two great countries,” Mr. Baumgartner said in a post on X.
Mr. Baumgartner also raised the issue of disruptions during Deepavali celebrations in his home state of Washington.

“A couple weeks back some attention-seeking racist morons disrupted a Diwali celebration in my home state of Washington. This evening, I was pleased to attend the Diwali celebration at the US Capitol,” he said.

The Deepavali celebrations were also attended by the U.S. Congresswoman-elect Pia Dandiya, Congresspersons Grace Meng, Suhas Subramanyam, Shri Thanedar, Nick LaLota, Jonathan Jackson, Raja Krishnamoorthi, Norma Torres, Pete Sessions, Deborah Ross, Buddy Carter, Michael Guest, among others.
Scott Colom, who scripted history by becoming the first black Senator from Mississippi in 146 years, also lit the traditional lamp at the Deepavali celebrations.

India should replace its "legacy ineffective Russian junk” with American weapons systems and also opt for Boeing aircraft over those manufactured by European Airbus Industries, a U.S. Congressman has suggested.

Michael Baumgartner, a Republican from Washington state, made the remarks at Deepavali celebrations on Capitol Hill on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) in the presence of Namgya Khampa, the Deputy Chief of Mission at the Indian Embassy in Washington.

“I was pleased to again express my thoughts that the more U.S. exports to India — from weapons systems to replace their legacy ineffective Russian junk to Boeing airplanes that are superior to Airbus to the world’s best lentils from the Palouse — the better it is for our two great countries,” Mr. Baumgartner said in a post on X.

Mr. Baumgartner also raised the issue of disruptions during Deepavali celebrations in his home state of Washington.

“A couple weeks back some attention-seeking racist morons disrupted a Diwali celebration in my home state of Washington. This evening, I was pleased to attend the Diwali celebration at the US Capitol,” he said.

articles.title: Economic losses from Indonesia fires could reach $30 billion, research shows
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Wildfires have burned through 7.1 million acres so far in 2026, according to the Nusantara Atlas deforestation monitor, an area 18 times the size of London

Wildfires that tore through Indonesian forest and peatland areas this year could cost the Southeast Asian country more than $30 billion, the co-author of a study on the subject said on Friday (November 20, 2026).

Losses of physical assets and from disrupted economic activity alone would cost an estimated 340 trillion rupiah ($18.6 billion), according to new research by the Jakarta-based Center of Economic and Law Studies (CELIOS).
That was equal to about 2.69% of Indonesia's GDP, the CELIOS report said.
It said additional health costs from acute respiratory infections caused by the wildfires on Indonesia's Borneo, Sumatra and Papua islands could be as high as 225 trillion rupiah ($12.3 billion).

"There are also economic costs borne by the public, both directly and indirectly," CELIOS director Nailul Huda, a co-author of the report, told AFP.
Wildfires have burned through 2.88 million hectares (7.1 million acres) so far in 2026, according to the Nusantara Atlas deforestation monitor, an area 18 times the size of London.
Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year's blazes have been particularly severe.

articles.title: Malaysia plans to resettle 10,000 Rohingya in Turkiye
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The announcement by Deputy PM Ahmad Zahid Hamidi comes a day after the UN's top court, in a landmark ruling, said that Myanmar committed genocide against the ethnic minority

Malaysia is seeking to resettle 10,000 Rohingya migrants in Turkiye as part of efforts to resolve a long-running refugee challenge involving foreign asylum seekers, the majority from Myanmar, a senior official said Friday (November 20, 2026).
The announcement by Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi comes a day after the UN's top court, in a landmark ruling, said that Myanmar committed genocide against the ethnic minority.

"Following my recent official working visit to the Republic of Turkiye, the Cabinet has agreed to a proposal to resettle 10,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia to Turkiye through a structured skills training programme," Mr. Hamidi said.

"I put forward this proposal as part of the government's efforts to address the situation of Rohingya refugees in Malaysia in a more coordinated, effective and humane manner," he said. Rohingya refugees will undergo a Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) programme in Turkiye which would last three to six months.
The training will focus on practical skills that are in demand among employers across various industries in Turkiye, Mr. Hamidi said.
"With these skills, participants will be better equipped to secure employment and contribute to Turkiye's economy, subject to the country's rules and regulations," Mr. Hamidi said in a statement.
On Thursday (November 19, 2026), the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, in its ruling, also ordered that refugees be given a safe passage home and awarded compensation.

Malaysia in late September repatriated about 1,500 Myanmar nationals under what authorities described as a voluntary programme, part of a scheme that rights groups warn could put migrants at risk by returning them to conflict-ridden Myanmar.
It was not immediately clear whether Rohingya refugees who would be selected for resettlement in Turkiye would also participate on a voluntary basis.
Mr. Ahmad Zahid however, said the initiative "is in line with the principles that guide the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in seeking lasting solutions for refugees".

articles.title: Rohingya in Bangladesh welcome UN court’s genocide verdict but say they want to go home to Myanmar
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: “The Rohingya have their own distinct culture, their own language, their own land and everything else that defines an ethnic group,” said a Rohingya community leader

Hundreds of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh sat in front of a big screen at their sprawling camp in Cox’s Bazar, watching the news from the Netherlands, where the U.N.'s top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

For many, the historic verdict on Thursday (November 19, 2026) represented a “small victory” — offering a glimmer of hope that someday they would be able to return safely to their homes in Myanmar, across the border from Bangladesh.
It was a landmark judgement, finding Myanmar responsible for the crime against the country’s ethnic Rohingya — the first time the court ruled that a state committed genocide.

A Rohingya refugee gives a thumbs up while another person holds a placard following the announcement of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) verdict, in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the minority Rohingya population, at a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, November 19, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

The Hague-based International Court of Justice also ordered Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow the Rohingya to return home safely, pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.

But it remains to be seen how much of the ruling can be implemented. The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.
There was no immediate reaction to the ruling from the Myanmar delegation in The Hague or from the government in Myanmar.
At the refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Rohingya refugees told The Associated Press of their concerns.

Mohammad Rofik, a Rohingya community leader at the camp, said the verdict was “a victory” for them as it recognised the genocide and the sufferings of their minority in the Buddhist-majority nation, but that it was “not an end” to their ordeal.
“Justice has started,” Mr. Rofik said, adding that the Rohingya still have “a long way to go.”

articles.title: South Korea confirms first case of cholera in 10 years
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: It is the country's first case of cholera since 2016, when authorities identified three cases suspected to be caused by contaminated seafood. At least 162 people got sick in a larger outbreak in 2001
South Korea on Friday reported its first case of cholera in 10 years, with health authorities urging people to take precautionary measures, use only safe water and wash their food properly.

The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency said health workers confirmed cholera from test samples of a person who had visited a hospital emergency room in the southeastern port city of Changwon earlier this month, showing symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea.

The agency said the unidentified person, who recovered and was discharged on Tuesday, had not travelled overseas in the past two months. It said health workers were trying to trace the source of infection and the people the person had been in contact with.

It was the country's first case of cholera since 2016, when authorities identified three cases suspected to be caused by contaminated seafood. At least 162 people got sick in a larger outbreak in 2001.

The agency issued guidance urging people to stick to safe water and cooked food and to wash and peel fruits and vegetables. It also urged medical facilities to promptly test and report suspected cases.

articles.title: Tiger ‘Explorer’ reaches Mylavaram forest near Vijayawada; four villages on alert
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: GPS-enabled collar helps forest officials track the movement; no attacks on cattle or human habitations reported so far

The tiger ‘Explorer’, which has been roaming across the Eastern Ghats after travelling through several States, has entered the Mylavaram forest range in the Vijayawada forest division and was seen in the A. Konduru forest block on Friday (November 20, 2026), triggering a fresh alert among forest officials.

The tiger is staying in a hilly stretch with thick forest cover and dense bush growth. Forest officials are tracking its movements with the help of a GPS-enabled satellite radio collar fitted to it following its capture and subsequent release into the Papikondalu National Park earlier this year. Officials said the tiger had not entered any human habitation so far and no cattle deaths or attacks on livestock had been reported in the Mylavaram range.
The villages of A. Konduru, Cheemalapadu, Vinagadapa and Narkulapadu, located in the vicinity of the forest block, have been alerted as a precautionary measure.

Forest personnel are monitoring the animal's movements and keeping a safe distance to avoid disturbing it. Officials said its movement was being tracked continuously, though its next direction of travel could not be predicted.

The tiger was first noticed in the Nuzvidu range a couple of days ago and moved towards the Mylavaram range overnight. It has been staying in the A. Konduru forest block since the following morning. Officials said it could move back towards Nuzvidu or proceed towards other forest stretches, depending on its movement.

A five-member specialised tiger conservation team from Pune, which had assisted the Forest Department during earlier operations, is involved in monitoring the animal. The team is equipped to tranquilise and capture the tiger if the situation warrants it.
Forest Department personnel are also using GPS equipment, drones and camera traps to keep track of its movements.
The tiger, estimated to be about four to five years old, had earlier travelled through Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh and Telangana before entering Andhra Pradesh.
Believed to have originated in the Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve in Maharashtra , it was named ‘Explorer’ after its extensive journey across different forest landscapes.

After it strayed into human-inhabited areas in the Godavari region, the Forest Department launched an extensive operation to capture it. The ‘Explorer’ was tranquilised near Kurmapuram in Konaseema district on February 6 and subsequently released into the Papikonda National Park on February 14, after being fitted with a GPS-enabled satellite radio collar to monitor its movements.

articles.title: India’s smartphone sale plunged 22% during festive season
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The decline was much steeper than the pre-festive forecast of 12%. Market value, however, stayed broadly flat YoY, as ASPs grew 28% YoY, largely offsetting the fall in unit sales

As rising memory costs have been pushing smartphone prices to a new height, the impact of it was quite visible during the just concluded Indian festive season (October 8–November 10) which collapsed by an estimated 22% year-over-year (YoY), noted Counterpoint. The rising phone prices pushed a weaker demand as buyers held back their purchases.

“The decline was much steeper than the pre-festive forecast of 12%. Market value, however, stayed broadly flat YoY, as ASPs grew 28% YoY, largely offsetting the fall in unit sales,” the findings said.

The research firm highlighted that festive discounts narrowed to 10–25%, from 35–40% in 2025. “Even discounted entry-level models were generally priced higher than a year ago, putting upgrades out of reach for many price-sensitive buyers. Brands instead leaned on no-cost EMIs, bank offers and trade-ins, with 48% of smartphone sales being finance-led.”

During the first wave (October 8–18), volumes fell 19% YoY, with online sales falling short of the performance seen during earlier sale events. Online sales, which account for a significant share of smartphone purchases, declined as higher consumer traffic failed to translate into actual conversions.

During festive season also, Samsung had the best of lot with a 21% share, overtaking Vivo, as its sales fell 8% YoY against a 22% market decline. Galaxy S25 Ultra and Galaxy S25 drew strong demand, while Samsung delayed price hikes until after the sales and managed inventory better than rivals.
Vivo and Oppo declined 21% and 24%, respectively, holding up better in mainline retail through retailer incentives and bundled offers, but were weaker online.

Apple’s sales declined by double digits YoY despite strong feedback for the new iPhone 18 Pro series and continued consumer interest in the iPhone 17. However, refurbished iPhones saw strong demand as consumers sought more affordable options, which hurt demand for new iPhones.
Xiaomi declined sharply, though its sales picked up around Diwali, driven by the Redmi Note 15 and Note 17 series.
Google was the fastest growing brand in the ultra-premium segment (45,000+) as Google sold its highest ever pixel devices during festive season.
Brands with exposure to the sub-20,000 segment were hit hardest, declining by close to 50%.

Vivo and Oppo declined 21% and 24%, respectively, holding up better in mainline retail through retailer incentives and bundled offers, but were weaker online.

Apple’s sales declined by double digits YoY despite strong feedback for the new iPhone 18 Pro series and continued consumer interest in the iPhone 17. However, refurbished iPhones saw strong demand as consumers sought more affordable options, which hurt demand for new iPhones.

Xiaomi declined sharply, though its sales picked up around Diwali, driven by the Redmi Note 15 and Note 17 series.

Google was the fastest growing brand in the ultra-premium segment (45,000+) as Google sold its highest ever pixel devices during festive season.

articles.title: Rare ‘bridal veil’ bamboo mushroom spotted near Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A biologist stumbled upon the elusive and short-lived bamboo mushroom in Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary earlier this week.

S. Gagana, biologist and nature education officer at Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary in Srirangapatna, described the sighting amidst the woodland floor of the bird sanctuary on November 17 as a “delightful encounter.”

“With its dark cap, white stalk and delicate lace-like skirt, the mushroom looked like a tiny bridal veil amidst the forest floor. It was indeed a fortunate moment to witness this fascinating fungus in its natural habitat,” she said.
Scientifically known as Phallus indusiatus, the bamboo mushroom, popularly referred to as “veiled lady” or bamboo pith, derives its common name from its close association with bamboo thickets.

“However, it can also grow in other moist, shaded habitats rich in decaying leaves and organic matter. The net-like structure surrounding its stalk is called an indusium, which gives it the distinctive appearance of a veil,” Gagana explained.

Deputy Conservator of Forests (Mysuru Wildlife Division) Prabhu Gowda noted that the fungus grows on deadwood bamboo when moisture and temperature conditions are favourable, adding that it also emits a distinctive odour.

Interestingly, the bamboo mushroom is considered a delicacy in several Asian cuisines and is used in soups and stir-fries after proper processing. However, Gagana cautioned that wild mushrooms should never be consumed without expert identification.

C. Hemavathi, retired professor of Botany at Government First Grade College in Mysuru, confirmed the species identity, noting that while the fungus is not uncommon in wetter regions like Kodagu, its emergence in Ranganathittu’s riverine habitat is noteworthy.
“The sighting reminds us that Ranganathittu’s biodiversity extends well beyond its avian visitors, and even the forest floor holds fascinating wonders waiting to be discovered,” Ms. Gagana said.

articles.title: Guruvayur temple in Keralam to introduce special queue for women, mothers with infants
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: New darshan facility to come into effect on December 1; Devaswom plans to gradually shift queues outside the temple to ease congestion
Women devotees and mothers carrying infants will have a dedicated queue for darshan at the Guruvayur Sreekrishna temple from December 1.
The Guruvayur Devaswom managing committee has decided to introduce the special facility to make darshan more convenient for women and young children and ease congestion inside the temple.

Announcing the decision at a press conference on Friday (November 20, 2026), Devaswom chairman A.V. Gopinath said the initiative would provide considerable relief to women devotees and mothers who visit the temple with infants.

The move is also aimed at reducing overcrowding on the temple premises. The Devaswom plans to gradually shift as much of the existing queue system as possible outside the temple after conducting a detailed study, he said.
“We want to make Guruvayur a model temple for the world,” Mr. Gopinath added.

articles.title: Congress wants consultation on delimitation issue, accuses government of not reaching out
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Party proposes retaining 543 Lok Sabha seats, existing State-wise distribution and a 25-year freeze, with one-third reservation for women

The Congress party on Friday said it favoured resolving the issue of delimitation through consultations with all political parties, but accused the government of making no effort to engage the Opposition on the matter.

Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the party’s position was guided by a four-point formula: retaining the existing strength of 543 seats in the Lok Sabha; maintaining the present State-wise distribution of seats; reserving one-third (182) of the existing seats for women; and imposing a 25-year freeze on all three arrangements.

Mr. Ramesh said the need for an early consensus on the issue had become more pressing in view of of the fact that Article 82 of the Constitution will come into force and delimitation would be held once the results of the ongoing Census exercise are out early next year.
This could be unfavourable to some southern states – which have made progress in population control – and hence not feasible, he added.

articles.title: Air India, AI Express extend suspension of Jeddah flights till November 24
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Air India said passengers having confirmed bookings for travel to or from Jeddah up to November 24, made on or before November 20, may avail a complimentary rescheduling, subject to availability, or opt for a full refund upon cancellation
Air India and Air India Express on Friday (November 20, 2026) announced extending the suspension of flights connecting Jeddah till November 24 amid the prevailing security situation in Saudi Arabia.
The two airlines have already suspended services to and from Saudi Arabian cities Riyadh and Dammam till November 30.

"Due to the prevailing situation in the region, Air India and Air India Express flights to and from Jeddah will now be suspended until 24 November 2026. Flight operations to and from Riyadh and Dammam will continue to remain suspended until 30 November 2026," Air India said in a post on X.
Earlier, the services to Jeddah were suspended till November 21.

The airline said passengers having confirmed bookings for travel to or from Jeddah up to November 24, made on or before November 20, may avail a complimentary rescheduling, subject to availability, or opt for a full refund upon cancellation.
The provision also applies to guests holding confirmed bookings for travel to or from Riyadh and Dammam up to November 30, made on or before November 10, it added.
On November 18, IndiGo extended the cancellation of flights connecting Saudi Arabian cities till November 30.
Akasa Air has cancelled its flights to and from Riyadh and Jeddah till November 30.
Various Saudi Arabian cities and infrastructure have come under attack from Houthis in recent months.

articles.title: U.K., EU to announce youth mobility deal, as they discuss closer ties
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The two sides are expected to announce a scheme for 100,000 18-32 year olds to live and work across each other’s borders

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to agree new terms for Britain’s relationship with the EU as he meets with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on November 20 at a Summit meeting. Mr Burnham has said in recent weeks that Brexit had caused “more harm than good”.

The two sides are expected to announce a scheme for 100,000 18-32 year olds to live and work across each other’s borders. In addition, they are working on closer ties in food and drink and linking the carbon trading schemes of the U.K. and the EU, as per reports.
“There’s the possibility of lower food prices, I can’t turn my back on that,” Mr Burnham said.
The summit is expected to announce the start of a dialogue on migration — including returns of irregular migrants to third countries.

The deal is a significant step to closer ties but is not expected to be the post-Brexit “reset” with Brussels that the Labour Party has sought . Mr Burnham, who is taking forward some of the discussions held with Brussels by his predecessor Keir Starmer, has committed to keeping to the red lines outlined in the Labour 2024 manifesto for the duration of this parliament (2029).

These red lines include not joining the bloc, nor its customs union and single market, and not allowing the “free movement” of people across UK-EU borders. However, Mr Burnham has said the U.K. would have to decide on its long-term options for its ties with the EU — including rejoining the EU The nature of the future relationship between the U.K. and EU is likely to be a campaign issue when Britain approaches its next general election.
“Business across the country have been clear, our current deal with the EU is not good enough,” said UK minister for EU relations, Hamish Falconer.

Mr Burnham had earlier said he would present legislation to the U.K. Parliament next week on this week’s agreements with Brussels. The U.K. will need harmonize some of its laws with the EU’s (i.e., follow them) to operationalize any deal on agriculture for instance.

articles.title: FDA sets up council for post-market review of vaccines, gene therapies
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The FDA said the council is intended to improve accountability and transparency as biologic products grow increasingly complex, particularly in cell and gene therapy, a sector that has seen rapid regulatory expansion in recent years

The US Food and Drug Administration said on Thursday it had established a new internal safety body within its biologics center, formalizing independent oversight of approved products such as vaccines, gene therapies and blood products once they reach the market.

The CBER Safety Council will report directly to the director of the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, structurally separating post-market safety reviews from the offices responsible for approving those products, the agency said.

The council supersedes CBER’s existing Safety Working Group, bringing together senior scientific and regulatory officials to review safety signals, conduct benefit-risk assessments and recommend regulatory actions as warranted.

The new structure formalizes an independent post-market review process at a time when regulators face mounting pressure to closely monitor newer biologic products, including gene and cell therapies, after approval, when they are used across far broader patient populations.
Its mandate will cover emerging safety concerns, potential labeling changes, risk-management measures and safety-related post-market studies, as well as advising on potential market withdrawals.

The FDA said the council is intended to improve accountability and transparency as biologic products grow increasingly complex, particularly in cell and gene therapy, a sector that has seen rapid regulatory expansion in recent years.

The council will coordinate with external bodies including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Institutes of Health, drawing on surveillance systems such as the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) and the FDA Sentinel program.
The council takes effect on November 19; the agency said additional details on its structure and membership will be released later.

The FDA said the council is intended to improve accountability and transparency as biologic products grow increasingly complex, particularly in cell and gene therapy, a sector that has seen rapid regulatory expansion in recent years

The US Food and Drug Administration said on Thursday it had established a new internal safety body within its biologics center, formalizing independent oversight of approved products such as vaccines, gene therapies and blood products once they reach the market.

The CBER Safety Council will report directly to the director of the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, structurally separating post-market safety reviews from the offices responsible for approving those products, the agency said.

The council supersedes CBER’s existing Safety Working Group, bringing together senior scientific and regulatory officials to review safety signals, conduct benefit-risk assessments and recommend regulatory actions as warranted.

The new structure formalizes an independent post-market review process at a time when regulators face mounting pressure to closely monitor newer biologic products, including gene and cell therapies, after approval, when they are used across far broader patient populations.

Its mandate will cover emerging safety concerns, potential labeling changes, risk-management measures and safety-related post-market studies, as well as advising on potential market withdrawals.

The FDA said the council is intended to improve accountability and transparency as biologic products grow increasingly complex, particularly in cell and gene therapy, a sector that has seen rapid regulatory expansion in recent years.

The council will coordinate with external bodies including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Institutes of Health, drawing on surveillance systems such as the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) and the FDA Sentinel program.

The council takes effect on November 19; the agency said additional details on its structure and membership will be released later.

articles.title: Watch | How has ‘Project Cheetah’ progressed in India?
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A video explainer on 'Project Cheetah', the first intercontinental transfer of wild cats into the country.

In September 2022, Prime Minister Narendra Modi released a coalition of cheetahs into the Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh. Eight cheetahs, five of which are female, were flown from Windhoek, Namibia, to Gwalior.

It was the first intercontinental transfer of wild cats into India since independence. The proposal for the project, known as ‘Project Cheetah’, was prepared in 2008-09 under the then PM Manmohan Singh.

The cheetahs were flown into India following several weeks of medical supervision in Namibia. They will be released into the wild gradually so that they have enough time to adapt to Indian conditions.

It also ensures reduced risk of contracting and spreading infection and hone the skills to hunt Indian prey. The eight cheetahs were housed in six enclosures, referred to as ‘bomas’ and were initially provided with buffalo meat.

All are expected to be moved inside larger enclosures in weeks. The cheetahs are radio-collared and their movements will be tracked. Each animal also has a dedicated tracking team. A team of wildlife scientists, biologists and zoologists are monitoring the initiative.

articles.title: As Project Cheetah completes 4 years, big cat population in India rises to 52
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: India’s cheetah population has risen to 52, including 32 cubs born in the country, as Project Cheetah completes four years on September 17, 2026, with officials highlighting the survival of cubs, breeding success and the expansion of the animals into open forest areas as key milestones.
Cheetah brought from Botswana gives birth to four cubs at Kuno
On September 17, 2022, Prime Minister Narendra Modi released eight wild cheetahs from Namibia into special enclosures at Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh.
The next phase of the cheetah restoration programme involves expanding suitable habitat for cheetahs and establishing a comprehensive, long term cheetah meta population in India.

While 49 cheetahs are in Kuno National Park, three others are in Gandhi Sagar Sanctuary, both in Madhya Pradesh. Over the last four years, many important milestones have been achieved, ranging from the reintroduction of cheetahs to breeding, survival of cubs and expansion into open forest, an official said in a statement.
The journey that began in Namibia on the distant African continent has now reached Gandhi Sagar Sanctuary. A total of 32 cheetahs were born in India, officials said.

The success in cheetah breeding and expansion was achieved by learning from difficulties. “The team faced many challenges in the first year of cheetah reintroduction. During this time, they gained experience in cheetah behaviour, health, and management adapted to Indian conditions,” an official said.
In the next year, the focus shifted to the survival and development of cubs born in India. According to the document, 13 cubs survived for more than a year after birth.

In the third year, 2025, cheetahs were released into open forest areas. They were monitored 24 hours a day across an interstate landscape spanning 12 districts, officials said, adding that the cheetahs gradually adapted to new areas.
The establishment of breeding females and the successful survival of the second generation of cubs in the fourth year are considered significant achievements of the programme, they said.

fullParagraphs: U.S., China, Russia must draw up a roadmap for talks on nuclear weapons

The first trilateral summit between the Presidents of China, the U.S. and Russia , held in Shenzhen on November 19, reflected both the changing global order and the leaders’ shared desire to remain engaged with one another in an increasingly unpredictable world. For U.S. President Donald Trump, the summit was a platform where he could push for joint talks between the world’s three largest nuclear powers on reducing nuclear warheads. After the New START treaty between the U.S. and Russia expired in February 2026, Moscow had signalled that it was ready for talks, but Mr. Trump wanted to involve China as well. For President Xi Jinping, the summit reinforced China’s position as a peer competitor to the U.S. While Russia seeks to deepen partnership with China, the U.S. is looking to build strategic stability. And for Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the West sought to isolate after he launched the invasion of Ukraine, the summit offered a seat at the high table. The decision to start trilateral talks on nuclear arms and the joint declaration, which stated that ‘a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought’, are steps in the right direction. But much will depend on what follows.

Many had compared the meet to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when Russian leader Joseph Stalin, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to discuss the future of post-War Europe. But Shenzhen was not a summit of the victors of a major war. This was more about three great powers setting terms of engagement in a changing world. The summit failed to achieve any breakthrough on any of the issues on the agenda — nuclear arms reduction, non-proliferation or the Ukraine war — or even offer a road map for the future. Moreover, it is not clear if the Shenzhen spirit could be sustained in the medium to long-term as another President in the U.S. could take a very different approach towards Russia and China. The three leaders have called for reform of the UN. While it is a welcome move, any attempt to reform the international system and institutions must also involve other powers, particularly rising middle powers such as India, South Africa and Brazil. But the Shenzhen framework could bring greater stability and predictability to great-power relations. This is important given that two of the Big Three are currently waging two separate wars. The leaders should draw up a clear road map for nuclear talks and other key issues outlined in the Shenzhen declaration, with realistic and achievable objectives. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.
